Question: Battery reports (mobile devices)
Answer: On Windows, powercfg /batteryreport produces an HTML report comparing design capacity with full charge capacity. macOS shows battery condition under System Settings. Phones show battery health under settings.

Question: Storage health (mobile devices)
Answer: S.M.A.R.T. data from the drive or vendor tool.

Question: Thermal behavior (mobile devices)
Answer: Fans constantly at full speed, or throttled performance, point to dust or dried thermal paste.

Question: Stylus (mobile devices)
Answer: Active styluses need power (battery or charging) and pairing. Passive styluses work on any capacitive screen.

Question: Headsets, speakers, webcams (mobile devices)
Answer: Usually Bluetooth or USB. Check that the OS has selected the right input and output device.

Question: Trackpad, drawing pad, track points (mobile devices)
Answer: Alternative pointing devices. A drawing pad is also called a graphics tablet.

Question: SIM (mobile devices)
Answer: The physical subscriber identity card. eSIM is an embedded, reprogrammable SIM activated by QR code or carrier app. Many phones support two lines using one SIM and one eSIM.

Question: Hotspot (mobile devices)
Answer: Shares cellular data over Wi-Fi. Carriers may cap or block hotspot data.

Question: GPS (mobile devices)
Answer: Satellite positioning, most accurate outdoors, uses more battery.

Question: Cellular location services (mobile devices)
Answer: Triangulation from cell towers, works indoors, less precise.

Question: Business applications (mobile devices)
Answer: Mail, cloud storage, and line-of-business apps, usually delivered by MDM.

Question: Mail (mobile devices)
Answer: Configure with the account type (Exchange/Microsoft 365, IMAP, POP3), server names, ports, and security settings. Most corporate mail uses modern authentication, not a typed server address.

Question: Cloud storage (mobile devices)
Answer: OneDrive, Google Drive, iCloud. Watch for storage limits and sync conflicts.

Question: Contacts and calendar (mobile devices)
Answer: Usually synced through the mail account.

Question: Recognizing data caps (mobile devices)
Answer: Photo and video sync over cellular can burn through a plan. Set sync to Wi-Fi only.

Question: Calendar and contacts (mobile devices)
Answer: Duplicates usually mean the same account was added twice, or two sync sources were enabled for the same data.

Question: Business vs personal accounts (mobile devices)
Answer: Keep them separate. MDM may block copying data from work apps to personal apps.

Question: Regulations (networking)
Answer: Each country's regulator decides which channels and power levels are legal. That is why a router has a country setting.

Question: Channel selection (networking)
Answer: Pick channels that do not overlap with neighbors. A Wi-Fi analyzer shows what is in use.

Question: Channel width (networking)
Answer: 20, 40, 80, 160 MHz, and 320 MHz on Wi-Fi 7. Wider channels are faster but more likely to overlap. On a crowded 2.4 GHz band, stick to 20 MHz.

Question: Bluetooth (networking)
Answer: Short-range personal area network. Low Energy (BLE) variants power fitness trackers and beacons.

Question: NFC (networking)
Answer: A few centimeters. Contactless payment, badge readers, quick pairing.

Question: RFID (networking)
Answer: Radio tags read at a distance. Inventory, toll tags, access badges. Passive tags have no battery and are powered by the reader.

Question: SCADA (networking)
Answer: Supervisory control and data acquisition. Controls industrial processes such as power grids, water treatment, and factories. Often old, hard to patch, and should be isolated on its own network.

Question: IoT devices (networking)
Answer: Smart thermostats, cameras, speakers, sensors. Weak default passwords and rare updates. Put them on a separate VLAN or guest network.

Question: VLAN (networking)
Answer: Splits one physical switch into several logical networks. Keeps guest, IoT, voice, and staff traffic apart. Traffic between VLANs must pass through a router or Layer 3 switch.

Question: VPN (networking)
Answer: An encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network. Site-to-site VPNs join offices. Client VPNs let remote workers reach internal resources.

Question: PoE switch (networking)
Answer: Powers devices directly from its ports. Check the total power budget.

Question: PoE injector (networking)
Answer: Adds power to one cable when the switch does not support PoE.

Question: APIPA (networking)
Answer: A Windows client that cannot reach DHCP gives itself a 169.254.x.x address. It can talk to other APIPA hosts on the same segment, but not to the internet. Seeing APIPA almost always means a DHCP problem.

Question: Subnet mask (networking)
Answer: Separates the network part from the host part. 255.255.255.0 (/24) is the SOHO default: 254 usable hosts.

Question: Default gateway (networking)
Answer: The router address. Without it, a host can reach only its own subnet.

Question: SATA (hardware)
Answer: Thin 7-pin data cable, separate 15-pin SATA power connector.

Question: eSATA (hardware)
Answer: External SATA. Shielded, no power (unless eSATAp). Largely replaced by USB 3 and Thunderbolt.

Question: Spindle speeds (hardware)
Answer: 5,400 rpm (quiet, low power), 7,200 rpm (desktop standard), 10,000 and 15,000 rpm (enterprise). Faster spin means lower latency.

Question: Form factors (hardware)
Answer: 3.5-inch (desktops, NAS) and 2.5-inch (laptops, some servers).

Question: M.2 (hardware)
Answer: Small card that plugs straight into the motherboard. Keyed M (PCIe x4, NVMe), B (SATA or PCIe x2), or B+M (fits both). An M.2 SATA SSD in a slot that supports only NVMe will not be detected, and the reverse is also true. Check the motherboard manual.

Question: mSATA (hardware)
Answer: An older, smaller card form factor for SATA SSDs.

Question: Flash drives (hardware)
Answer: USB. Often FAT32 or exFAT for cross-platform use.

Question: Memory cards (hardware)
Answer: SD, microSD, CompactFlash. Cameras and phones.

Question: Optical drives (hardware)
Answer: CD (700 MB), DVD (4.7 GB single layer, 8.5 GB dual layer), Blu-ray (25 GB per layer). Mostly legacy, still used for archives and some software installs.

Question: CPU architecture (hardware)
Answer: x86/x64 (Intel, AMD) dominates PCs. ARM (Apple silicon, Qualcomm Snapdragon, phones) is more power efficient. Software built for one architecture needs translation or recompiling to run on the other.

Question: Core configurations (hardware)
Answer: Multiple cores run tasks in parallel. Hyper-threading (Intel) and SMT (AMD) present two logical threads per core. Many modern CPUs mix performance cores and efficiency cores.

Question: Virtualization support (hardware)
Answer: Intel VT-x or AMD-V must be enabled in firmware to run 64-bit VMs well.

Question: TPM (hardware)
Answer: A chip (or firmware function) on the motherboard that stores keys and measures boot integrity. BitLocker stores its key here. Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0.

Question: Fans (hardware)
Answer: Case fans set airflow (usually front intake, rear and top exhaust). CPU fans sit on the heat sink.

Question: Heat sink (hardware)
Answer: Metal fins that pull heat from the CPU or GPU.

Question: Thermal paste/pads (hardware)
Answer: Fill microscopic gaps between the chip and heat sink. Replace paste whenever you remove a cooler. Use a pea-sized amount.

Question: Liquid cooling (hardware)
Answer: A pump moves coolant from a block on the CPU to a radiator. Quieter under load, but pumps can fail and leaks are possible.

Question: Printer share (hardware)
Answer: A PC shares a locally connected printer. Depends on that PC being on.

Question: Print server (hardware)
Answer: A server hosts the queue, drivers, and permissions for many printers. Better for businesses.

Question: Benefits (virtualization cloud)
Answer: Central management and patching, data stays in the data center, works on cheap or personal devices, fast recovery if a laptop is lost.

Question: Costs (virtualization cloud)
Answer: Depends on the network. Poor latency means a poor user experience. Server and licensing costs move to the back end.

Question: Examples (virtualization cloud)
Answer: Azure Virtual Desktop, Amazon WorkSpaces, Citrix, VMware Horizon.

Question: End of life (EOL) (operating systems)
Answer: No more security updates. EOL systems are a security risk and fail compliance checks.

Question: Update limitations (operating systems)
Answer: Old hardware may not meet new OS requirements (Windows 11 needs TPM 2.0), so the device is stuck on an EOL OS.

Question: Application and driver support (operating systems)
Answer: Confirm apps and drivers work on the new version (backward compatibility).

Question: Hardware compatibility (operating systems)
Answer: Check CPU, TPM, RAM, and storage against requirements.

Question: Feature updates and product life cycle (operating systems)
Answer: Windows gets an annual feature update. Each version has its own support end date.

Question: Domain vs workgroup (operating systems)
Answer: A workgroup has local accounts on each PC. A domain has central accounts and policy in Active Directory.

Question: Upgrade paths (operating systems)
Answer: Home to Pro is an in-place license upgrade. Moving to a different architecture (32-bit to 64-bit) needs a clean install.

Question: Sleep/suspend/standby (operating systems)
Answer: Keeps RAM powered, resumes in seconds, uses a little battery.

Question: Hibernate (operating systems)
Answer: Writes RAM to disk (hiberfil.sys) and powers off. Slower to resume, no battery use.

Question: Fast startup (operating systems)
Answer: A partial hibernate of the kernel at shutdown. Can hide driver problems and block dual-boot access to the disk. Turn it off when troubleshooting.

Question: USB selective suspend (operating systems)
Answer: Powers down idle USB devices. Disable it when USB devices disconnect randomly.

Question: Printers (operating systems)
Answer: Add by IP, by share name, or through a print server.

Question: File servers and mapped drives (operating systems)
Answer: Map with File Explorer (Map network drive) or net use. The path format is a UNC path: \\server\share.

Question: Static vs dynamic (operating systems)
Answer: Static for servers and printers, DHCP for clients.

Question: Alternate configuration (operating systems)
Answer: A fallback static address when DHCP is unavailable.

Question: VPN (operating systems)
Answer: Built-in client (IKEv2, SSTP, L2TP) or a vendor client.

Question: Proxy settings (operating systems)
Answer: Manual proxy or automatic configuration script (PAC). A wrong proxy setting breaks web browsing while ping still works.

Question: Public vs private network (operating systems)
Answer: Public hides the PC and blocks discovery. Private allows discovery and sharing. Choose public for coffee shops.

Question: Metered connections (operating systems)
Answer: Windows limits background downloads and updates. Useful on cellular and hotspots.

Question: File Explorer network paths (operating systems)
Answer: Type \\server\share in the address bar.

Question: Kernel (operating systems)
Answer: The core that manages hardware, memory, and processes.

Question: Bootloader (operating systems)
Answer: Loads the kernel at startup (GRUB is common).

Question: systemd (operating systems)
Answer: The init system and service manager on most distributions. Manage services with systemctl start|stop|status|enable .

Question: Root account (operating systems)
Answer: The superuser. Avoid logging in as root. Use sudo for single commands.

Question: Defender Antivirus (security)
Answer: Built in. Activate or deactivate (it disables itself when a third-party antivirus is installed), and update definitions (through Windows Update or manually).

Question: Defender Firewall (security)
Answer: Activate or deactivate per profile, configure port security (allow only needed ports), and application security (allow specific apps).

Question: Joining a domain (security)
Answer: System properties, needs a Pro or higher edition and domain admin (or delegated) credentials.

Question: Assigning a log-in script (security)
Answer: Runs at sign-in, often to map drives.

Question: Moving objects within organizational units (OUs) (security)
Answer: Moving a user or computer to another OU changes which Group Policy applies.

Question: Assigning home folders (security)
Answer: A personal network folder for each user.

Question: Applying Group Policy (security)
Answer: Linked to sites, domains, or OUs. Refresh with gpupdate /force.

Question: Selecting security groups (security)
Answer: Assign permissions to groups, not individuals.

Question: Configuring folder redirection (security)
Answer: Stores Documents and Desktop on a server, so they follow the user and get backed up.

Question: Third-party vendor (security)
Answer: A certified destruction or recycling company.

Question: Certificate of destruction/recycling (security)
Answer: Proof for auditors that media was destroyed.

Question: Regulatory and environmental requirements (security)
Answer: Data regulations (HIPAA, GDPR, and similar) and e-waste laws.

Question: Change default passwords (security)
Answer: The first thing to do.

Question: IP filtering (security)
Answer: Allow or block by address.

Question: Firmware updates (security)
Answer: Fix vulnerabilities.

Question: Content filtering (security)
Answer: Block categories of websites.

Question: Physical placement/secure locations (security)
Answer: Keep the router where visitors cannot reset it.

Question: UPnP (security)
Answer: Lets devices open ports automatically. Convenient but abused by malware. Disable unless needed.

Question: Screened subnet (security)
Answer: Formerly DMZ. A zone for public-facing devices, separate from the internal network.

Question: Configure secure management access (security)
Answer: HTTPS only, disable remote (WAN-side) administration.

Question: Encryption settings (security)
Answer: WPA3 or WPA2-AES with a long passphrase.

Question: Guest access (security)
Answer: A separate network, isolated from internal devices.

Question: Port forwarding/mapping (security)
Answer: Send inbound traffic on a port to one internal device (such as a camera DVR or game server). Forward only what is needed.

Question: Frequency (operational procedures)
Answer: Set by how much data the business can afford to lose.

Question: In-place/overwrite recovery (operational procedures)
Answer: Restore over the original location. Fast, but overwrites current versions.

Question: Alternative location recovery (operational procedures)
Answer: Restore somewhere else, compare, and then move. Safer when unsure.

Question: Proper battery disposal (operational procedures)
Answer: Lithium-ion and other batteries go to battery recyclers, never the trash.

Question: Proper toner disposal (operational procedures)
Answer: Return programs or recyclers. Toner is a fine powder, so clean spills with a toner vacuum.

Question: Other devices and assets (operational procedures)
Answer: E-waste regulations apply to PCs, monitors, and phones. Remove and destroy data first.

Question: NDA/MNDA (operational procedures)
Answer: Non-disclosure agreement (one-way) and mutual NDA (both parties).

Question: Regulatory and business compliance requirements (operational procedures)
Answer: Rules the organization must meet.

Question: Splash screens (operational procedures)
Answer: Log-in banners that state authorized use and monitoring, supporting legal action later.

Question: Appearance (operational procedures)
Answer: Match the attire of the environment: formal or business casual.

Question: Language (operational procedures)
Answer: Avoid jargon, acronyms, and slang. Explain in plain terms.

Question: Attitude (operational procedures)
Answer: Positive, confident.

Question: Listen actively (operational procedures)
Answer: Do not interrupt. Take notes.

Question: Be culturally sensitive (operational procedures)
Answer: Use appropriate professional titles.

Question: Be on time (operational procedures)
Answer: If you will be late, contact the customer.

Question: Avoid distractions (operational procedures)
Answer: No personal calls, texting, social media, or personal interruptions.

Question: Difficult customers (operational procedures)
Answer: Do not argue or get defensive. Do not dismiss their issues. Do not be judgmental. Clarify by asking open-ended questions, restating the issue, and confirming understanding. Do not post about customer experiences on social media.

Question: Set and meet expectations (operational procedures)
Answer: Give timelines and status updates. Offer repair or replacement options. Provide documentation of the services. Follow up later to verify satisfaction.

Question: Confidential and private materials (operational procedures)
Answer: Do not read, copy, or discuss documents on the customer's computer, desk, or printer.

Question: Unintentionally introducing malware (operational procedures)
Answer: Only run scripts from trusted sources. PowerShell execution policy and code signing help.

Question: Inadvertently changing system settings (operational procedures)
Answer: Test in a sandbox or VM first.

Question: Browser or system crashes due to mishandling of resources (operational procedures)
Answer: A loop that never ends, or one that eats memory, can hang a machine.
